paragraphs.source_en: Why were some sites selected and others not? It is difficult to determine the reason purely on the basis of the landscape morphology since painted sites often have the same characteristics as empty sites. However, the painted sites present various morphologies which may have influenced the kind of activities done there. Can the type of paintings indicate the type of activity that occurred there? Today, it is not possible to establish a direct link between a painting and a ritual or ceremony which occurred in the site, but differences between compositions in various sites are evident. Sefar, the largest site with the greatest number of paintings is a stone city hidden inside surrounding rocks. There are at least four figures of Great Gods surrounded by groups of humans in a worshipping posture, which might indicate the use of the site for religious purposes.

paragraphs.source_en: Tin Mzghigauin in the northern Tassili is a rock shelter on a hill above a huge plain and therefore visible from faraway. Except for two very small anthropomorphic figures the shelter is dominated exclusively by largesized images of wild animals, such as antelope, a warthog and an elephant. The position of the shelter may have influenced the paintings and the reason for their creation; when present in the shelter, hunters could easily observe all the animals on the underlying plain. Indeed, when compared with the paintings at Sefar, there is little that is mysterious about the quite realistic animals at Tin Mzghigauin, although their creation was probably not as simple as copying real animals.

paragraphs.source_en: Sometimes two or more painted sites are visible from each other. Jabbaren and Aouarnhat are two stone cities located on opposite banks of a deep wadi (Fig. 3-9). Since its banks are very steep and high, the access from one site to the other was rather difficult, if not impossible, when the river was flowing in prehistoric times. However, the two sites seem to be related because the main painted shelters at Aouarnhat are situated at its external part and oriented towards Jabbaren. At Jabbaren paintings are present only in the side of the stone city nearest to the wadi and therefore nearer to Aouarnhat.
